# Incident Report: 2024-08-15-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap

## Summary

A Windows workstation on the `10.8.15.0/24` LAN browsed to a fake package-tracking site, which delivered a ZIP containing a heavily padded malicious JScript file (a **GootLoader-style** loader, behaviorally attributed). Minutes later the host abused Windows BITS to pull down a second-stage Windows PE64 DLL payload from an attacker-controlled bare IP, then beaconed to that same IP for roughly 30 minutes with encrypted HTTP POST/GET traffic.

## Victim host

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 address | `10.8.15.133` |
| MAC address | `00:1c:bf:03:54:82` (confirmed via ARP and Ethernet source on the host's own traffic) |
| Windows hostname | `DESKTOP-H8ALZBV` (NBNS, DHCP option 12, mDNS) |
| Logged-in user | `plucero` (Kerberos `CNameString`, AS-REQ/TGS-REQ traffic to the domain controller) |
| AD domain | `lafontainebleu.org`, DC `WIN-JEGJIX7Q9RS` at `10.8.15.4` |
| LAN gateway | `10.8.15.1` (DHCP option 3) |

## Malware family

**GootLoader** (initial JS loader) — **behavioral attribution, not signature-confirmed.** No IDS/Suricata alert export was present in the evidence directory, so this is based purely on traffic/artifact behavior:

- The lure delivered a ZIP containing `Invoice-876597035-003-8331775-8334138.js`, a **7.0 MB** JScript file. Its content is >99% garbage padding assembled from scraped legitimate document/report text (MPI standard documentation, IPCC/OECD/PIAAC report text) wrapped around a single `WScript` call. Bloating a JS dropper to multiple megabytes with scraped document text is a distinctive, well-documented GootLoader technique used to defeat sandboxes and AV size/heuristic checks.
- This is consistent with GootLoader's known chain: JS executed via `wscript.exe` → downloads/loads a second-stage Windows payload.
- The second-stage payload retrieved via BITS is a PE32+ DLL with internal PDB path `E:\work\ooooooops\181\knock_v1.1.8\knock\bin64\knock.pdb` (internal name `release.dll`), which sets up a `CreateMutexW` single-instance mutex and links `WS2_32.dll` (networking) — consistent with a loader/RAT component, though this specific "knock" project could not be named further from traffic alone.
- The follow-on C2 channel (raw HTTP to a bare IP, static spoofed legacy `MSIE 6.0` user-agent, `Cookie:`-carried encoded token, large encrypted POST bodies) matches generic commodity loader/RAT beacon behavior, not a specific signature I can confirm from this evidence alone.

## Indicators of Compromise (all observed directly in the capture)

**Delivery / initial access**
- Malicious lure domain: `quote.checkfedexexp.com` (Cloudflare-fronted, resolved IP `104.21.55.70`)
- Related lure domain (same campaign infrastructure, contacted via TLS shortly after): `business.checkfedexexp.com` (Cloudflare-fronted, resolved IP `172.67.170.159`)
- Malicious URL: `http://quote.checkfedexexp.com/managements?16553a25e45250a41fd5&endeds=MIGpq&JStx=59bf050d37df88a9-ade43358-eaa1220b-0571422b-0f33e6aa150e86bafd0ed4&Ld=9d7502d88d752a27b1d00587309184b5a215` — HTTP GET returned a ZIP archive directly (Chrome/Edge 127 user-agent)
- Dropped archive contents: `Invoice-876597035-003-8331775-8334138.js` (7,000,020 bytes)
- SHA256 (ZIP archive as transferred): `798563fcf7600f7ef1a35996291a9dfb5f9902733404dd499e2e736ea1dc6fc5`

**Second-stage payload / C2**
- Command-and-control endpoint: **`72.5.43.29:80`** — sole C2 IP, contacted directly (no DNS lookup, hardcoded IP), ~1,827 seconds of sustained beaconing (304 GET, 1 HEAD, 3 POST requests)
- Payload delivered from C2 via abused BITS (`Microsoft BITS/7.8` user-agent): `http://72.5.43.29/data/0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4`
- Transferred file: `0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4` — PE32+ executable (DLL), x86-64
- SHA256: `b7aec5f73d2a6bbd8cd920edb4760e2edadc98c3a45bf4fa994d47ca9cbd02f6`
- Internal build path (PDB): `E:\work\ooooooops\181\knock_v1.1.8\knock\bin64\knock.pdb`
- Beacon fingerprint: spoofed user-agent `Mozilla / 5.0 (compatible; MSIE 6.0; Windows NT 5.1; SV1; .NET CLR 1.0.3705)` (note the non-standard space before the slash), encoded token in `Cookie:` header, large encrypted POST bodies (total ≈306 KB exfiltrated/uploaded across 3 POSTs)

**Benign context, not indicators** — for completeness, ruled out as attacker infrastructure: Microsoft/Windows telemetry and Delivery Optimization traffic (`*.microsoft.com`, `*.msn.com`, `*.bing.com`, `msedge.b.tlu.dl.delivery.mp.microsoft.com` — legitimate Edge extension/update CDN downloads), Adobe update check (`acroipm2.adobe.com`), OCSP revocation checks (`oneocsp.microsoft.com`), and normal AD/DC traffic (LDAP, Kerberos, CLDAP, DRSUAPI to `10.8.15.4`).

## Recommended actions
- Isolate `10.8.15.133` (`DESKTOP-H8ALZBV`) from the network immediately.
- Reset credentials for user `plucero` and review the domain controller for any lateral use of those credentials.
- Block `72.5.43.29` and the `checkfedexexp.com` domains at the perimeter/DNS layer.
- Hunt the environment for the two file hashes above and for the mutex/PDB artifact `knock_v1.1.8`.
